newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet alleges dangerous cargo was disguised.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet alleges dangerous cargo was disguised.

text.p: ValuJet Airlines Inc. said on Thursday that maintenance company SabreTech Corp. deliberately disguised dangerous cargo suspected of causing the May 1996 crash of Flight 592 in the Florida Everglades.

ValuJet said it had asked the National Transportation Safety Board to investigate what it called "significant evidence" before issuing a final conclusion about the cause of the crash, which killed all 110 people aboard the DC-9.
The NTSB is to release its final report on the crash on Aug. 19. Preliminary reports have blamed a fire in the cargo hold that was fueled by oxygen generators carried there.
The NTSB's report also is expected to be critical of both ValuJet and SabreTech, the maintenance contractor that handled the oxygen generators.

"ValuJet believes there is significant evidence pointing to some SabreTech employees deliberately and deceptively packaging, mislabeling and illegally shipping cargo which they knew was dangerous," ValuJet said.
It alleged that SabreTech employees may have falsified shipping documents "because they believed the process of proper disposal and transport of the generators would take too much time."
SabreTech denied ValuJet's allegations. "There is no evidence whatsoever that anyone deliberately deceived ValuJet," Kenneth Quinn, legal counsel for SabreTech, said.

"It's a thinly diguised effort to delay and discredit the NTSB report. And it's no coincidence that it comes on the eve of ValuJet's day of reckoning," he said. "SabreTech has acknowledged many mistakes. It's unfortunate that ValuJet has not."

ValuJet said it had provided the information, discovered by attorneys working for the airline, to the NTSB, the Federal Aviation Administration, the Federal Bureau of Investigation and the federal prosecutor in Miami.

"Significant questions related to this accident remain unanswered," the airline said. "Because of the pending criminal investigation of SabreTech and its employees, the SabreTech personnel involved with the handling, packaging and shipping of the oxygen generators have taken the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination."

"As a consequence, the NTSB and the public have only gotten half the story," ValuJet said. SabreTech acknowledged that a criminal investigation was ongoing but said it has provided all relevant information to investigators.

ValuJet said its cargo policy prohibits the transport of oxygen generators on company aircraft. Since the crash of Flight 592, the FAA has banned oxygen generators as cargo from passenger flights in the United States.

ValuJet alleged that a SabreTech shipping clerk, when preparing shipping documents for the oxygen generators carried aboard Flight 592, instructed another SabreTech employee to list the generators as "oxy canisters - empty."

When the generators were delivered to Flight 592 by SabreTech, they were packed without protective materials, in unmarked boxes without required warnings or other disclosures of their contents, according to the airline.
SabreTech said it did not know that the generators were hazardous and did not package the shipment. "The packaging, the labeling, that was their responsibility," Quinn said.
SabreTech sued ValuJet in May, asserting ValuJet had to indemnify SabreTech for damages related to the crash.
ValuJet Airlines' parent company agreed last month to merge with AirWays Corp., parent of AirTran Airways, to form a company called AirTran Holdings Inc.
